Revival plan for sick fertilizers units 
*181.    SHRIRAJEEVSHUKLA: 
DR. M.A.M. RAMASWAMY: 
Will the Minister of CHEMICALAND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government are working on a proposal to revive 
eight sick or closed public sector fertilizer factories in the country; 
(b) if so, the details of the proposal and estimated time frame alongwith the 
cost for the revival; 
(c) whether the revival of these factories will be sufficient to meet the 
growing demand of fertilizers in the country; and 
(d) if not, in what way Government propose to meet the excess demand? 
2 

[4 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI RAM 
VILAS PASWAN): (a) to (b) Yes, Sir. The following units of fertilizers Public 
Sector Undertakings are closed: 
(i)       The Fertilizer Corporation of India Ltd. Talcher 
Korba 
Ramagundam 
Sindhri 
Gorakhpur 
(ii)      Hindustan Fertilizer Corporation Ltd. Durgapur 
Haldia 
Barauni 
(iii)      Pyrites, Phosphates & Chemicals Ltd. Amjhor 
Dehradun 
Saladipura 
Government is exploring the possibilities of revival of the closed units of 
fertilizers Public Sector Undertakings. Since the matter is at an exploratory 
stage, the details are not worked out, in respect of the closed units. 
The sick units of fertilizers Public Sector Undertakings are Fertilizer and 
Chemicals Travancore Limited (FACT) and Madras Fertilizers Limited (MFL). In 
respect of sick unit of FACT, a financial restructuring package has been 
sanctioned, and the possibilities of revival of MFL are under examination. 
(c) to (d) while, in the event of revival, these units will contribute to 
fertilizer supply, other measures, such  as debottlenecking/expansion/Joint 
Ventures abroad/Modernization are expected to take care of future demand. 
Malaria control in North Eastern Region 
*182 SHRI SILVIUS CONDPAN: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMINLY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether his Ministry has established a wing at Guwahati to control/ fight 
malaria epidemic affecting the lives of the people of North Eastern States every 
year resulting in loss of lives of poor villagers; 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [4 August, 2006] 
(b) what was the amount sanctioned during 2004-05 and 2005-06 for Assam 
to combat AIDS/ HIV cases; and 
(c) what are the actions taken by the State Government in this 
connection? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANI 
RAMDOSS: (a) to (c) The Government of India has established the office of 
Regional Director at Guwahati, Assam for supervision and monitoring of national 
health programmes including malaria and other vector borne diseases. This 
office is exclusively for Assam. In addition, Regional Directors have been 
posted at Shillong in Meghalaya and Imphal in Manipur for supervision and 
monitoring in other North Eastern States. 
In addition, Indian Council of Medical Research Institutions, viz., Field Unit 
of National Institute of Malaria Research at Sonapur, Assam and Regional 
Medical Research Centre at Dibrugarh, Assam, provide research inputs and 
technical guidance for prevention and control of malaria in N.E. States. 
To combat AIDS/HIV cases, an amount of Rs. 1214.50 lakh and Rs. 915.60 
lakh was sanctioned to the State in 2004-05 and 2005-06 respectively. 
Malaria: 
The following actions have been taken by the State Government:— 
• The Government has issued instructions to all the District Health 
Authorities to take preventive and co ntrol measures in their respective 
jurisdictions including difficult and inaccessible areas. 
• Staff deployment for ennancing surveillance of fever cases and their 
appropriate treatment, viz., mass fever spray through Mobile teams and 
mass radical treatment involving NGOs, Panchayati Raj Institutions, etc. 
• Drug Distribution Centres (DDCs), Fever Treatment Depots (FTDs) for 
facilitating early case detection and prompt treatment have been activated. 
• Instructions have been issued o the Deputy Commissioners to closely 
supervise and monitor Anti-Malarial activities by involving 
4 

[4 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
entire district machinery. They have  also been authorized to incur 
expenditure on account of mobility and other life-saving drugs from 
District Health Society (National Rural Health Mission). 
• Collaboraton with Tea Gardens has also been emphasized. 
• Implementing DOT Indoor Residual Spraying in all districts. 
• Fogging operations with Malathion (Technical) in urban areas. 
• Conducting mass impregnation of community owned bed nets. 
• Carrying out mass awareness on prevention and control of malaria through 
print media by issuing handouts, advertisements and electronic media, 
miking, etc. 
• Deputing Medical Teams including Para-Medical staff to the most 
affected Lakhimpur and Golaghat districts from Assam Medical 
College, Dibrugarh and Guwahati Medical College, Guwahati as well as 
from Hospitals of other Districts and Directorate of Health Services. 
• Ensuring availably of insecticides and Anti-Malarial drugs in all districts. 
AIDS 
As in the rest of the country, the National AIDS Control Programme is a 
centrally sponsored scheme, implemented through Assam State AIDS Control 
Society with the following components:— 
• Preventive targeted interventions for high risk populations adopting a multi-
pronged strategy including peer counseling and behaviour change 
communication. A total of 27 interventions were under implementation as 
on 31-03-2006 in the State of Assam. 
• Preventive interventions for the general population through 
programmes for blood safety, voluntary counseling and testing services, 
Prevention of Parent to Child Tr ansmission (PPTCT), Information 
Education and Communication (IEC). Atotal of 29 counseling Centers, 
34 Blood Banks and 2 Blood Component Separation Units had been set up 
as on 31-03-2006 in Assam. 
• Provision of low cost care ad support services by providing community 
care services, treatment of opportunistic infections, free 
5 

RAJYA SABHA [4 August, 2006] 
Antiretroviral Therapy in designated centers and prevention of occupational 
exposure. 2 Community Care Centers and 1 Drop In Center have been 
established. A total of 107 patients are receiving free ART in the ART 
Centre in the State. 
• Collaborative efforts to promote inter-sectoral programme activities 
including work placed interventions and public-private partnerships. 
• Build technical and managerial capacities for programme implementation 
through Surveillance, Training, Monitoring and Evaluation, Technical 
resource Groups, operational research and Programme management. 
Security arrangements at stations 
† *183   SHRI KAMAL AKHTAR: 
SHRI SHAHID SIDDIQUI: 
Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that despite bomb explosions in Mumbai no strict 
arrangements of security on various railways stations including the capital have 
been made; 
(b) if so, whether it is also a fact that at the most important station of the 
capital, most of the door metal detectors are either out of order or not functioning 
properly; 
(c) if so, whether Government propose to take steps to improve the 
security arrangements on various railway stations including those of the 
capitals; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS (SHRI LALU PRASAD): (a) No, Sir. 
'Policing' being a State subject, registration of cases, their investigation, 
maintenance of law and order in Railway premises as well as on running trains 
and collection, collation and sharing of actionable intelligence are the statutory 
responsibility of the State Police. The State Police have a separate wing called 
the Government Railway Police (GRP) for dealing with all matters relating to 
law and order on the Railways. The State 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
6 

[4 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
Governments have made elaborate arrangements of security after the incidents 
of serial bomb blasts in Mumbai (Western Railway) on 11.07.2006. However, 
in addition to security measures taken by Government Railway Police and State 
Police, two additional Companies of Railway Protection Special Force (RPSF) 
have been deployed in Mumbai to supplement their efforts. Moreover, 
additional Railway Protection Force (RPF) personnel have also been 
mobilized to Mumbai from adjoining divisions in Western and Central 
Railway to strengthen the security measures at railway stations. Close Circuit 
Televisions (CCTVs) at 14 important and sensitive Railway stations have 
been installed to keep surveillance in Railway premises. 17 Sniffer dogs have 
been provided in Mumbai (Western and Central Railway) to conduct anti-
sabotage checking at Railway stations. 97 numbers of Hand Held Metal 
Detectors have also been povided to Railway Protection Force (RPF) and 
Railway Protection Special Force (R PSF) staff for conducting intensive 
checking at Railway stations in Mumbai. Similar preventive measures have also 
been adopted at various other important and sensitive Railway Stations over the 
country including Railway stations located at National Capital, Delhi. Close 
liaison with Govenment Railway Police and State Police authorities is being 
maintained to povide effective security to passengers and passenger area. 
(b) No, Sir. All available Door Frame metal Detectors, which were initially 
installed by Delhi Railway Police, are in working condition and being used for 
checking of passengers at the entry/ex it points. Whenever  any Door Frame 
Metal Detector develops technical snag and becomes dysfunctional, all efforts 
are made immediately to repair and make them functional again. 
(c) and (d) Yes, Sir. The following measures are being taken to improve 
security arrangements at important and vulnerable railway stations:— 
 
1. Installation of Close Circuit Televisions at vulnerable Railway Stations. 
2. Modern security gadgets like Hand Held Metal Detectors, Door 
Frame Metal Detectors, Entry S cans/X-Rays Machines etc. to 
strengthen access control at entry/exit points. 
3. Dog Squads, Bomb Detection and Disposal Squads at various 
divisions and railway stations to conduct anti-sabotage checks. 
7 

RAJYA SABHA [4 August, 2006] 
4. To upgrade training centers to improve quality of training to Railway 
Protection Force personnel. 
5. Intensive publicity and public awareness campaigns alerting and 
educating all passengers/public to remain vigilant against any 
unidentified/unclaimed suspicious objects lying on platforms, other 
premises or coaches and to report to RPF/GRP/Railway officials 
available nearby. 
6. Frequent announcements at all stations alerting passengers to be 
vigilant about suspicious movement of co-passengers and not to touch 
any suspicious luggage/bag especially in general compartments. 
7. Steps to prevent entry of unauthorized persons in trains and in empty 
coaching rakes at originating/destination stations, before and after 
placement in maintenance sidings. 
8. Close co-ordination with GRP/State Police/Centra! Intelligence 
agencies to prevent any untoward incident. 
9. The contact telephone numbers of concerned higher officers of 
Security Directorate, Railway Board have been inserted in All India 
Railway Time Table i.e. 'Trains—at—a—Glance" for assisting the 
passengers in need of immediate help. 
10 The Railways are also in the process of preparing contingency plans at 
the Divisional Railway level to deal with contingencies arising out of 
sudden bomb blasts. These plans w ill be put into operation jointly 
with the help of State Police and Government Railway Police (GRP). 
Stoppage of wastage and value addition under 
Horticulture Mission 
*184. SHRI EKANATH K.THAKUR: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Rs. 15,000 crore horticulture mission is 
8 

[4 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
taking big steps forward as agricultural scientists are coming up with do's and 
don'ts for preventing the colossal waste of fruits and vegetables in the country; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that agricultural scientists are working on the 
linkages for intensifying efforts for value addition in fruits and vegetables as part of 
the horiculture mission; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) to (c) 
A Centrally Sponsored Scheme on National Horticulture Mission (NHM) was 
launched during the Tenth Five Year Plan, commencing from 2005-06 with a total 
outlay of Rs. 2300.00 crore for the Plan period for the holistic development of 
the horticulture sector covering production, post harvest management and 
marketing, with the active participation of all stake holders. 'In principle approval has 
also been given for implementing the Scheme during the Eleventh Five Year Plan 
with an outlay of Rs. 15,000.00 crore The Scheme has provision for setting up 
infrastructural facilities for post harvest management, such as pack houses, 
cold storages, Controlled Atmosphere (PA) storages, refrigerated 
vans/containers and mobile processing units for increasing the marketability of 
the horticulture produce, adding value to the produce, increasing profitability and 
reducing losses of the produce. 
Technologies for such infrastructure developed by the institutions under the 
Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) and Council of Scientific and 
Industrial Research (GSIR), besides Horticulture Departments under the State 
Agricultural Universities (SAUs) are being transferred to he farmers and 
entrepreneurs. 
For proper linkage between research and development on all aspects of 
horticulture, including post harvest management and value addition, a 
Research Advisory Committee has been envisaged under NHM with the 
involvement of Scientists of ICAR, CSIR, SAUs and other Research 
organizations. 
9 

RAJYA SABHA [4 August, 2006] 
Second Green Revolution 
† *185   DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI: 
SHRI MANGANI LAL MANDAL: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Ch airman of National Commission of 
Farmers, Dr. M.S. Swaminathan has underlined the need for Second Green 
Revolution in the country; 
(b) if so, the facts in this regard; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that there is need of making dry land or land 
dependent on rain useful upto the maximum level in order to bring Second Green 
Revolution in the country; 
(d) if so, the reaction of Government thereto; and 
(e) the scheme being prepared by Government for Second Green Revolution? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) and (b) 
The National Commission on Farmers has recommended, inter alia, 
introduction of an integrated package of measures to increase farm productivity 
and profitability. The package recommended by the Commission consists mainly 
of five components, namely, (a) soil health enhancement through concurrent 
attention to the physics, chemistry and microbiology of the soils; (b) water 
harvesting, water conservation and sustainable and equitable use of water; (c) 
access to affordable credit, and crop and life insurance reforms; (d) development 
and dissemination of appropriate technologies; and (e) improved opportunities, 
infrastructure and regulations for marketing of produce 
(c) and (d) The integrated and holistic development of rainfed areas 
constitutes one of the important components of the strategy formulated by the 
Government to increase agricultural production and productivity. There are 
several schemes in operation to chieve this objective. These include (i) the 
National Watershed Development Project for Rainfed Areas; (ii) the River Valley 
project and Flood prone River Programme; and (iii) the Watershed Development 
Project in Shifting Cultivation Areas. Recently the Government launched the 
scheme entitled "Micro Irrigation" which 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
10 

[4 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
aims at water conservation with enhanced efficiency, especially relevant to 
rainfed areas. 
It has also been decided to set up a National Rainfed Area Authority 
(NRAA) to, inter alia, prepare a prospective plan and evolve policy guidelines for 
development of Rainfed/Dryland Farming System. 
(e) The Government is following a multi-pronged strategy to maximize 
agricultural production and productivity through programmes designed to 
promote resource conservation technol ogies; enhancement in seed re-
placement; balnced use of fertilizer; in-situ moisture conservation; and 
enhanced water use efficiency. The emphasis is also to promote crop 
diversification and follow a regionally differentiated strategy based on the agro 
climatic conditions for accelerating crop output growth. 
Vacancies in Indian Council of Agricultural Research 
*186.    SHRIMATI SYEDA ANWARA TAIMUR: 
SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) how many posts of scientific nature are vacant in the Indian Council of 
Agricultural Research; 
(b) the reasons for not filling these posts; 
(c) whether keeping so many posts vacant has not hindered the progress of 
various research schemes; and 
(d) how long it would take to fill all these vacant posts? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) Pres-
ently there are 1462 vacancies in the scientific cadre at the Indian Council of 
Agricultural Research (ICAR). 
(b) Filling up of vacancies was affected by the restrictions imposed by 
department of Personnel & Training Office Memorandum dated 16 05.2001. 
(c) and (d) The work has been managed by judicious redeployment of 
available manpower. Enhancement of the age of superannuation of Scientists in 
ICAR from 60 to 62 years from October, 2003 also helped to reduce the 
shortfall. Steps have been initiated to get all vacancies in the scientific cadre 
filled up on top priority basis.

Directives for participation of corporates in 'Green Drive' 
*188. SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHAR JEE: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether on the World Environment Day, Government had given a call to 
corporates to play a greater role in 'Green Drive' in a whole range of issues from 
forestry to naming affluent plants and monitoring pollution; and 
(b) if so, the response of different sectors of industry, like pesticides, dyes 
and chemicals, pharmaceuticals, distilleries, cement, mines and metals, to this 
directive? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) 
On the occasion of World Environment Day, Government organized a 
Colloquium on Corporate Responsibility for Environmental Protection in 
association with Confederation of Indian Industry (Cll) in which the 
representatives of the Government, and Industry participated. The 
Colloquium underlined the need for more active response by the corporate sector 
towards environmental protection. 
(b) Recognizing the merit, cost effectiveness and long-term sustainability 
of voluntary compliance and self-regulation, the Government 
13 

RAJYA SABHA [4 August, 2006] 
had introduced Charter on Corporate Responsibility for Environment 
Protection (CREP) in March, 2003. The CREP covers 17 categories of highly 
polluting industries, and is being guided by 8 tasks forces in the 
implementation of the Charter. The interactive and consultative process 
sustained over this period has resulted in an acknowledged recognition of the 
fact on the part of industry that preventive pollution control measures are 
economically more viable as compared  to the curative measures. There has 
been a mixed response from the industry. While industries like aluminium, 
cement and thermal power plants have adopted improved environmental 
practices, industries like pesticides, dyes and dye intermediates, distilleries, 
and pharmaceuticals have yet to give the desired response.

Crashworthy impact reducing coaches 
*195. SHRI B.J. PANDA: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government propose to bring out "crashworthy" i.e. impact-
reducing coaches with anti-climbing features to reduce the impact of collision and 
provide maximum safety to the passengers; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the time-frame within which these coaches would be added to the rakes 
to control loss of life and property in rail accidents? 
THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS (SHRI LALU PRASAD): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Indian Railways used wooden bodied passenger coaches till early 1950's 
when the metal body 'Integral Shell' design for passenger coaches was adopted. 
This design had anti-telescopic features and the sections at doorways were 
deliberately made weaker so that in the event of a impact or collision, the damage 
would occur in lavatory/doorway and the passenger portion would be reasonably 
safeguarded. 
To further improve upon the crashworthiness of coaches, a design of a coach 
shell has been developed which will have certain crash elements at the ends for 
absorbing a part of impact energy in the event of collision. This design not only 
enhances the energy absorbed at the collision interface but also enables bulk of the 
remaining energy being transferred to the next coach interface in the train formation 
so that a significant amount of energy of impact is absorbed at the next coach to 
coach connection, thus enhancing passengers safety. This design is based on use 
of centre buffer 
19 

RAJYA SABHA [4 August, 2006] 
coupler arrangement for connection of coaches in a train formation. Use of tight 
lock Centre buffer coupler which is an essential element of this design, also provides 
anti-climbing feature so that in the event of collision, coaches do not pile on top of 
each other. This also reduces chances of injury and loss of human life. 
(c) Based on initial design, one rake has been manufactured and is in service 
between Amritsar, Barauni and Saharsa. This rake consists mainly of llnd Class 
coaches as till now, the design details have been finalized only for llnd Class 
coaches. For other type of coaches, designs are expected to be finalized in next few 
months. More rakes will be provided with these features progressively.

farmers; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) and (b) The Commission for Agricultural 
Costs and Prices is entrusted with the task to advise on recommendations of 
Minimum Support Prices (MSPs) of agricultural commodities, including 
foodgrains, keeping in view (i) the need to provide incentive to the producer for 
adopting improved technology and for developing a production pattern broadly in 
the light of national requirements; (ii) the need to ensure rational utilization of land, 
water and other production resources; and (iii) the likely effect of the price policy 
on the rest of economy, particularly on the cost of living, level of wages, 
industrial cost structure, etc. 
Apart from making a comprehensive overview of the entire structure of the 
economy of a particular commodity, the CACP considers the cost of 
production, changes in input prices, input/output price parity, trends in market 
prices, demand and supply situation, inter-crop price parity, effect on industrial 
cost structure, effect on general price level, effect on cost of living, internatinoal 
market price situation, parity between prices paid and prices received by 
farmers (Terms of Trade) while formulating its recommendations on price 
policy. Besides, the Commission undertakes field visits for close interaction with 
farmers in different parts of the country. 
(c) and (d) By and large, the Government concurs with the 
recommendations but at times improves upon the recommendations. A 
statement indicating the MSPs of foodgrains recommended by CACP and fixed by 
Government since 2002-03 is enclosed in Statement-I (See below). 
(e) and (f) the Government announces each season Minimum Support Prices 
(MSPs) for major agricultural commodities and organizes purchase operations 
through public and cooperatives agencies such as Food Corporation of India 
(FCI), Jute Corporation of India (JCI), Cotton Corporation of India (CCI), National

(a) whether the decision to import wheat reflects Government's failure to

DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHARAD PAWAR): (a) The procurement of wheat in 
Rabi Marketing Seasons (RMS) 2005-06 was 147.87 lakh tonnes white the off-
take of wheat in 2005-06 was 171.64 lakh tonnes. As a result the stocks of 
wheat in the Central Poof as on 1st January, 2006 was 61.88 lakh tonnes 
against the buffer norm of 82 lakh tonnes.

open market prices of wheat, a decision was taken to import 5 lakh tonnes of 
wheat in February, 2006. Subsequently/in RMS 2006-07, it was estimated that 
only 95 lakh tonnes of wheat would be procured against the estimate of 162 lakh 
tonnes. Therefore, to augment the wheat stocks in the Central Pool, since the

agencies carry out. Minimum Support Price (MSP) operations in wheat

Government agencies or private traders, including large private companies, as is 
advantageous to him.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER

and (b) Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) is operating product certification scheme 
primarily on voluntary basis. So it is not essential for production companies to 
comply with the Indian Standards of BIS. However, 110 product including Packaged

Packaged Natural Mineral Water without ISI Mark is taken by the designated 
State Health Authorities under the provision of Prevention of Food Adulteration 
Act and Rules framed thereunder. However, if BIS receives information about such 
companies manufacturing the product without having appropriate and valid 
certification marks licence from it, the Appropriate Authority in the concerned 
State Government is informed for taking necessary enforcement action 
against the offenders. At the instance of BIS, the State Government of Andhra 
Pradesh launched an intensive drive wherein about 403 units have been prosecuted

1233. SHRI PENUMALLIMADHU: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is noted in a seminar that about eight lakh children are 
105 

RAJYA SABHA [4 August, 2006] 
born with birth defects in India every year and it is mainly due to uncontrolled 
environmental degradation; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) According to the National 
Neonatal-Perinatal Database Report supported by Indian Council of Medical

critically polluted areas.

1239. SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are planni ng to separate the National Parks 
Services from Indian Forest Service; 
116 

[4 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) what are the reasons that compel  to bifurcate the Ministry of 
Environment and Forests; 
(d) what are the key points on which Government would focus while 
formulating the proposal; 
(e) on what criterion Government  would divide/accommodate the 
employees working in the Ministry; and 
(f) how much time Government would take to complete the proposal? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS (SHRINAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) and (b) Presently a National 
Parks Service does not exist. However, proposals are being formulated for creating 
a National Parks Service as a new All India Service. The details of the proposal 
shall be worked out in consultation with the State Governments as per the 
constitutional provisions and provisions of the All India Services Act, 1951. 
(c) There is no proposal to bifurcate the Ministry of Environment and 
Forests. However, to give a focused attention to Forests and Wildlife issues, there is a 
proposal to create a separate Department of Forests and Wildlife within the 
Ministry of Environment and Forests. 
(d) The key points of focus in the proposal are that:— 
(i) The programs/schemes which are being implemented in the field by the 
State Forest Departments are proposed to be brought in the fold of 
Forests & Wildlife Department. 
(ii) The officers of Indian Forest Service would be considered for senior policy 
making positions including that of a Secretary in the new Department 
of Forests and Wildlife. 
(e) Standard norms of distribution of staff shall be followed in the division of 
employees of the Ministry of Environment and Forests between the two 
Departments. 
(f) For creation of a National Parks Service, the finalization of the proposal shall 
depend on completion of formalities of consultations with the State

Deforestation of Himalayas 
1245. SHRI EKANATH K. THAKUR: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a biodiversity and conservation expert has warned 
that rapid deforestation in parts of Himalayas could lead to the extinction of 
hundreds of plants, dozens of birds and animal species; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the fore st cover on the Indian side of the 
mountain range would fall from 84.9 per cent in 2000 to 52.8 per cent by 2100 if 
nothing is done to reduce unchecked development and land clearing for farming; 
and 
(c) if so, the steps Government propose to take to check the deforestation of 
Himalayas? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) to (c) No specific 
information has come to the notice of the Ministry. In general rapid 
deforestation causes loss of habitat, which leads to extinction of fauna & flora. 
Forest Survey of India, an organization under the Ministry of Enviroment & 
Forests, Government of India carries out the assessment of the forest cover of 
the country on a biennial basis. FSI has not analysed forest cover in the mountain 
range of Indian side separately. As per State of Forest Report 2003, the forest 
cover in the Himalayan States of Jammu & Kashmir, Himachal Prades, 
Uttaranchal, Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh is 131,366 Sq. Km. which is 31.11%

measures to check deforestation in Himalayas: 
(i) Administrative measures: Patrolling of forest area, Network of 
Checkposts, Mechanism of Transit Permits for movement of forest 
produce, Control and regulation of saw mills, Restrictions on movement of 
timber in North-Eastern Region as per the directions of Hon'ble Supreme 
Court 
(ii) Legal measures: Indian Forest Act, 1927, Wildlife (Protection) Act, 
1972, Forest Conservation Act, 1980 and Environment Protection Act, 
1986 and the rules, guidelines thereof. 
(iii) Management measures: Working of forests according to approved 
Working Plans, involvement of local people in protection and 
managment.

under Central Sector and Centrally Sponsored Schemes and Externally 
Aided Projects.

Statement 
Guidelines for promotion of Indian Forest Service Officers 
With a view to addressing stagnation in the Indian Forest Service at various 
levels in different cadres, and removi ng the inter-cadre disparities, following 
guidelines are made in continuation of the earlier guidelines issued vide the 
letter No. 20019/01/2000-IFS (II) dated 18th November, 2002. 
2. The State/UT Government shall ensure that the Screening Committees that 
have been provided for in the earlier guidelines for considering promotion of 
IFS officers, shall meet at least six months in advance from the date from when 
a particular batch of the officers becomes due for promotion to higher grades. 
Since the completed years of the service are reckoned from 1st of January, it is 
suggested that Screening Committee Meeting shall be held by July-August every 
year and a report to this effect shall be sent to the Cadre Controlling authority 
in this Ministry. 
3. In such Screening Committee Meetings all the officers of a particular batch 
that becomes due for promotion to higher grade shall be considered and all the 
officers recommended by the Committee shall be granted higher scale in one 
go, on the due date by the State Government/UT. 
(i)(a). For promotion to the grade of Principal Chief Conservator of 
Forests (PCCF), if there are not sufficient vacancies to accommodate all 
129 

RAJYA SABHA [4 August, 2006] 
eligible officers, the State/UT Government shall under Rule 9(7) of the IFS (Pay) 
Rules 1968, create equivalent number of ex-cadre posts as included in the senior 
duty posts and accommodate the officers against those posts. 
(ii) (a). If number of officers in a batch is more than the total number of cadre 
and ex-cadre posts which can be available for this level, the State/ UT  
Government may forward proposals to this Ministry for obtaining 'no-objection' 
for creation of more ex-cadre posts for a specified period. 
(b) In the case of the officers who have completed 25 years of service or more 
and have not been promoted to the level of Additional PCCFs due to insufficient 
vacancies, the State/UT Government ma y create required number of ex-cadre 
posts for granting promotion to all the eligible officers to the grade of Addl. 
PCCF. 
(c) In the case of officers having 18 years of service or more and have not 
been promoted to the scale of Chief Conservator of Forests (CCFs) due to 
insufficient vacancies, the State/UT Government may create required number of ex-
cadre posts for granting promotion to all the eligible officers to the grade of CCF 
(d) In the case of officers who have co mpleted 14 years of service and yet 
to be promoted to the scale of Conservator of Forests (CF), due insufficient 
vacancies, the State/UT Government may create required number of ex-cadre 
posts for granting promotion to all the eligible officers to the grade of CF. 
(e) In the case of officers who have co mpleted 13 years of service and 
have not been granted selection grade, may be granted selection grade in 
relaxation of restrictions on availability of number of posts for grant of 
selection grade as it is only a non-functional scale. 
4. The State/UT Governments shall make all efforts to utilize the State-
Deputation Reserve (SDR) and the Central Deputation Reserve (CDR) by deputing 
officers to various departments in the State/UT Governments and forwarding 
nominations of suitable officers to the Central Government for consideration for 
central deputation. 
130 

[4 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
5. The State/UT Governments shall foresee the overall requirement of IFS 
Cadre while formulating their Cadre Review proposals and the Cadre Review 
proposals shall be so worked out as to ensure smooth career progression of IFS 
officers.

Steps to control diabetes 
1255. SHRI MAHENDRA MOHAN: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have reviewed a recent compilation of the World Health 
organization on global deaths from diabetes, highlighting inter-alia 
140 

[4 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
that in India some 39.9 million people are afflicted with diabetes and that one in 
five Indian dies of the disease; and 
(b) if so, the details of any specifi c awareness programme/strategy with 
action-plans drawn up to inform and sensitize the public to the dangers of the 
disease and other suitable steps initiated to help in controlling the disease? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) As per World Health 
Organisation (WHO) estimates there were 31,705,000 people with diabetes in India 
in 2000. According to the revised estimates of WHO (2004), there are 32 million 
diabetics in India and the WHO (2002) has projected that India would have 
largest number of diabetics (80 million) in the world by 2030. 
(b) The Government proposes to initiate and implement a National 
Programme for the prevention and control of diabetes, Cardio-vascular diseases 
(CVD) and Stroke to reduce the adverse health impact of diabetes, heart diseases and 
Stroke. Under this proposed National programme IEC will be one of the major 
components to sensitise the public about the dangerqus effect of these diseases 
and its prevention. 
Maternal mortality 
1256. SHRI MAHENDRA MOHAN: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have reviewed a recent report of the UNICEF 
highlighting inter-alia that the maternal mortality ratio (MMR) in India is as high 
as 540 maternity deaths per 1,00,000 births, and that there has been no significant 
reduction in the MMR over the last six years; 
(b) if so, the details of other major conclusions/observations contained in the 
UNICEF report and the action taken/proposed to be taken thereon; 
(c) the details of maternal mortality ra tio recorded in different States 
during the last five years; and 
(d) the specific scheme(s) launched, if any, to help to achieve safe 
motherhood? 
141 

RAJYA SABHA [4 August, 2006] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKS HMI): (a) to (d) As per the 
UNICEF report on maternal mortality in the year 2000, the MMR in India is 540 
per 1,00,000 live births. This figure on estimated maternal mortality rate is 
based on the findings of National Family Health Survey-ll. However, based on the 
official estimates of Registrar General of India (RGI) for 1998 the maternal 
mortality rate was estimated as 407 per 100000 live births. As per the estimation 
from RGI for the year 2004 the Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) is 50 per 1,000 live 
births for India. 
The UNICEF report observed that India accounts for more than 20% of global 
maternal and child deaths and also records 20% of the births world wide. 
Approximately 30 million women in India experience pregnancy annually and 
27 million are live births. 
State wise and year wise data on the number of maternal deaths is not 
available. However, Maternal Mortality Rates as estimated for major states by the 
Registrar General of India for the year 1997 and 1998 (Sample Registration 
System) are given in statement. (See below) 
The Government has planned to reduce the maternal and infant mortality in the 
country. As per the National Population Policy-2000 and National Health 
Policy-2002, the goal for reduction in maternal mortality rate has been kept at 
less than 100 per 100,000 live births and infant mortality rate is to be brought 
down to 30 per 1,000 live births. Government of India is actively pursuing these 
goals under the National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) in order to improve the 
availability of and access to quality health care including Services for 
Immunization and Safe Motherhood. The mission seeks to provide effective 
health care to rural population throughout the country with special focus on 18 
States, which have weak public health indicators and/or weak infrastructure. 
These States are Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Himachal 
Pradesh, Jharkhand, Jammu & Kashmir, Manipur, Mizoram Meghalaya, 
Madhya Pradesh, Nagaland, Orissa, Rajasthan, Sikkim, Tripura, Uttaranchal 
and Uttar Pradesh. The Mission will ope rate over a period of seven years 
from 2005 to 2012. Under the NRHM, the services provided under the RCH 
Programme will be strengthened through: 
• Implementation of the Janami Suraksha Yojana (JSY) under which cash 
incentives and services are provided to pregnant women belonging to 
families Below Poverty Line (BPL). In case of Institutional delivery, in the 
low performing States benefits under the scheme is available to Non-BPL 
Pregnant Women also. The age bar and number of birth criteria has also 
been removed in these States 
142 

[4 August, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
• Appointment of Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHA) for every 
village with a population up to 1 000. ASHA will facilitate in accessing 
health care services to the community and will have specific responsibility of 
mobilizing pregnant women for antenatal care, institutional delivery and 
post-natal checks and immunization to children. 
• Operationalising 2000 Community Health Centres as First Referral Units 
(FRU) for providing Emergency Obsetetric and Child Health services. 
• Making 50% Primary Health Centers functional for providing 24-hours 
delivery services, over the next five years. 
• Ensuring quality of services by implementing Indian Public Health 
Standards (IPHS) for Primary Healthcare Facilities. 
• Ensuring skilled attendance at every birth both in the community and the 
Institutions. 
• The specific initiatives for reducing IMR are Integrated management of 
Neonatal and Childhood Illness (IMNCI), control of death due to acute 
respiratory infections (ARI), Control of diarrhea Diseases, provision of 
Essential New-Born Care, Prevention and Treatment of Micronutrient 
Deficiencies namely Vitamin A a nd Iron, exclusive breastfeeding and 
Immunization.

Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether to strengthen India's public health system, two world class public 
health schools are proposed to be set up in the country to begin with;

156

(b) whether these States also top in death rate; and

financially and physically to improve  their health-care infrastructure to 
control this menace? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) Yes, as per the latest 
available report from the office of th e Registrar General of India (Sample 
Registration System Bulletin April, 2006), Madhya Pradesh has the highest 
Infant Mortality Rate in the country,(79 per 1000 live births), followed by 
Orissa (77 per 1000 live births) and then Uttar Pradesh (72 per 1000 live 
births). 
(b) Yes, as per the latest available report from the office of the Registrar 
General of India (Sample Registration System Bulletin April, 2006), the crude 
death rate in the country is highest in Orissa (9.6 per thousand), followed by 
Madhya Pradesh (9.2 per thousand) and Uttar Pradesh (8.8 per thousand) 
(c) The Reproductive and Child Health (RCH) Programme being 
implemented all over the country places  special attention on Newborn and 
Child Health. The newborn health strategy envisages presence of Skilled 
Birth Attendant at the time of delivery, continuum of care from antenatal 
(period of pregnancy) to postnatal period (after pregnancy) and from home care 
to the facility based management. Thus there is to be a link between 
implementation of maternal and newborn health interventions. The Government of 
India shall also implement the Integrated Management of Neonatal and 
Childhood Illnesses (IMNCI) strategy through the Department of Health & 
Family Welfare and the Ministry of Women & Child Development. 
The National Rural Health Mission, operationalized throughout the 
country from the current financial year, subsumes all health programmes 
including RCH. It aims to provid e accessible, affordable, accountable, 
effective and reliable primary health care specially to poor and vulnerable 
sections of the population.

Reduction in steel production by producers 
† 1328. SHRI RAM JETHMALANI: 
SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD: 
Will the Minister of STEEL be pleased to state:  
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
225 

RAJYA SABHA [4 August, 2006] 
(a) whether it is a fact that the big steel producers had reduced the quantum 
of steel production during the last years in order to check the declining prices 
of the product on the basis of demand and supply of steel in the country; 
(b) if so, the facts in this regard; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that the cost of production is brought down by 
increasing the production in the industry and the common consumer as well as 
the producer are benefited thereby; and 
(d) if so, Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF STEEL (DR. 
AKHILESH DAS): (a) and (b) No Sir. The major steel companies have not 
reduced the quantum of steel production in the last few years. The production 
of five major steel producers has been given below:—  
Name of Product in Million Tonnes As%age of 2003-04 
Company  2005-06 2004-05 2003-04 2005-06 2004-052003-04

RINL Saleable Steel 3.237 3.173 3.169 102.14 100.12 100.0 
TISCO Saleable Steel 4.551 4.074 4.076 111.7 100.0 100.0 
Ispat Hot Rolled Steel 2.144 1.963 1.614 132.8 121.6 100.0 
JVSL Hot Rolled Steel 2.148 1.783 1.573 136.6 113.4 100.0 
Essar Steel Hot Rolled Steel 2.577 2.324 1.930 133.5 120.4 100.0 
There was a marginal drop in the production of TISCO in 2004-05 over 2003-
04 because the company had shut down their major blast furnace to renovate the 
same to a higher capacity. 
(c) and (d) As a general principle, higher production would lead to lowering 
of fixed costs per unit of output up to a certain level of production. However, in 
an open market scenario, steel prices are market driven. Cost reduction measures 
are taken up by steel companies as an ongoing process so as to increase 
productivity. This helps both the producers as well the consumers. The steel 
plants under Ministry of Steel are already working beyond their rated capacity.
